selectedTitle: How Planet Fitness Fits 7,200 Members Into One Gym
hookCandidates: Planet Fitness has 20.8 million members. Its ideal customer may be someone who barely walks through the door.
650 million workouts sounds enormous until you divide it by 20.8 million members.
Why would a gym be fine with you staying home?
Look at this 20,000-square-foot room. Now picture 7,200 people who each own a key to it.
A gym that sells more memberships than it can hold has an odd relationship with your attendance.
Planet Fitness gets paid whether you work out or not, and the filing says over 90% of its club revenue works that way.

beats.text: Planet Fitness has 20.8 million members. Its ideal customer may be someone who barely walks through the door.

That isn't a joke about New Year's resolutions. It's arithmetic. The company's own annual report implies roughly 7,200 members per club, and a club only has so much room. Here is how I got there, and where the report stops and my math begins.
Start with what the filing says. At the end of 2025, Planet Fitness reported about 20.8 million members and 2,896 clubs. Franchisees own 2,604 of those clubs. The company runs 292.
A typical club, the report says, is about 20,000 square feet. Hold on to that number.
Divide the members by the clubs and you get about 7,200 per location. That division is mine, not the company's. But it means roughly 7,200 people holding a key to the same 20,000 square feet.
If they all turned up on a Monday evening, nobody could move. So how many actually come? The annual report has one figure that gets us close.

It says members completed more than 650 million workouts in the company's clubs in 2025. Spread that over about 20 million members on average and you get roughly 2.7 workouts per member per month. That average includes everyone who never came. The report doesn't define a workout, so treat 2.7 as a rough floor, not a precise count.

Now bring it down to a single club. Using an average of about 2,800 clubs, 650 million workouts works out to around 230,000 per club per year. That is roughly 630 on a typical day, out of about 7,200 members. Fewer than one in ten walks in on a given day.

Compare that with what people say they will do. A well-known study followed 7,752 members at three health clubs. Those on a flat monthly fee of over $70 went about 4.3 times a month, which the authors calculated as more than $17 per visit, when a ten-visit pass would have cost $10 a visit.

Those clubs weren't Planet Fitness, so the study shows a pattern, not a measurement. But apply even that modest rate to 7,200 members and a club would see about 1,000 visits a day. The annual report implies about 630.

Here is the design problem. Floor space, machines and staff are fixed. Dues are charged per person. A club can spread its costs across thousands of members because, on any given day, only a few hundred use the room. That is the logic, and it is my reading of the numbers. Planet Fitness doesn't say it.

Look at how the company charges. The Classic Card starts at $15 a month for new members. The PF Black Card is $24.99. There is a $49 annual fee on top, and 66.5% of members were on the Black Card at the end of 2025.
Cancelling is where the contract matters. The filing says members may cancel at any time after giving proper notification, though some memberships carry an initial minimum term.

The report also says over 90% of both franchise and corporate-club revenue is recurring: royalties, monthly dues and annual fees. That kind of revenue doesn't depend on who shows up on a particular Tuesday.

Then there is who receives the money. Franchisees own most clubs, and the 10-K puts the average royalty they pay Planet Fitness at 6.7% of dues. They also contribute about 2% to national advertising funds. And they must buy their equipment from the company, replacing it every five to nine years, depending on club volume.

Does the 7,200 figure hold up? Here is a check. At the lowest price, $15 a month plus the $49 annual fee, 7,200 members pay about $1.6 million a year. At Black Card prices, about $2.5 million. The filing says clubs open more than a year average about $2.0 million. That sits inside the range. It doesn't prove the model, but it suggests the numbers are in the right neighborhood.

The company does describe how its clubs are built. Because they are typically 20,000 square feet and skip things like group classes and pools, it says there is more room for the equipment members use, and it hasn't needed to put time limits on cardio machines. It is the closest the report comes to talking about capacity.

None of this proves anything improper, and nothing in the filing says the model depends on members staying home. That is a conclusion from arithmetic, and the arithmetic has limits. A workout is undefined, the club count is an average, and heavy users offset the members who never come.

There's one more clue in the pricing. From 1998 until 2024 the Classic Card cost $10 a month. In May 2024 the company said new members would pay $15, and existing members kept their old rate. So the change reached the business slowly, one new signup at a time.

So when you pass a Planet Fitness on a weeknight and the lot looks half empty, that is not necessarily a sign of trouble. It may be the design. A club priced like this works best if most of its members, most of the time, are somewhere else.

dossier.researcher: Claude (web research session); every source below was opened and read for the cited facts on the date shown
dossier.thesis: Planet Fitness can charge a very low price partly because its clubs are sized for the share of members who actually show up, and the company's own filings point to that share being small.

contradictions.note: Planet Fitness does not state anywhere in the 10-K that its model depends on non-attendance, and the 10-K gives no members-per-club or capacity figure. Resolution: the video presents the capacity logic as OUR arithmetic on disclosed numbers (inferences i1-i3), not as a company statement, and says so on screen and in narration.
'Workouts' in the 10-K is undefined (check-ins vs distinct sessions). Resolution: use only as an approximate floor ('more than 650 million') and say the definition is the company's.
The academic study covers three non-Planet-Fitness health clubs (1997-2000), so it shows a behavioral pattern, not Planet Fitness behavior. Resolution: attributed only as a general finding.

The 10-K's capacity paragraph (c11) describes layout and equipment space, not attendance or members per club. It is cited only for what it says; it is not presented as the company confirming the non-attendance logic.

claims.text: At December 31, 2025 Planet Fitness had approximately 20.8 million members and 2,896 clubs (2,604 franchised, 292 corporate-owned); a year earlier, 19.7 million members and 2,722 clubs.
The FY2025 10-K says members completed more than 650 million workouts in the company's clubs.
The 10-K describes its clubs as typically 20,000 square feet.
Classic Card dues start at $15 a month for new members and the PF Black Card at $24.99; the standard annual fee is $49; Black Card penetration was 66.5% at year-end 2025.
Over 90% of both corporate-owned club and franchise revenues were recurring: royalties, monthly dues and annual fees.
In a study of 7,752 members at three health clubs, members on a flat monthly fee of over $70 attended on average 4.3 times a month, paying over $17 per expected visit versus $10 on a 10-visit pass.
The Classic Card cost $10 a month from 1998 until the May 2024 announcement that new members would pay $15; existing members kept their $10 rate.
The FY2025 10-K says clubs open more than 12 months had average unit volumes of approximately $2.0 million.
The 10-K puts Planet Fitness's average franchise royalty rate at 6.7% (63% of clubs at the current rate), and franchisees contribute approximately 2% of dues to national advertising funds.
Franchisees must buy equipment from Planet Fitness (or required vendors in some international markets) and generally replace it every five to nine years, based on club volume.

The 10-K says that because clubs are typically 20,000 square feet and omit amenities such as group exercise classes and pools, there is more space for equipment members use, and the company has not needed time limits on cardio machines.
The 10-K says members may cancel at any time after giving proper notification, and for certain memberships subject to an initial minimum term.

inferences.text: 20.8 million members across 2,896 clubs is about 7,200 members per club.

650 million workouts over 2025 spread across roughly 2,800 average clubs is about 230,000 workouts per club per year, or roughly 630 a day (workouts are defined by the company and the average-club count is approximate).
650 million workouts across about 20 million average members is about 2.7 workouts per member per month, counting members who never come.
If every member visited at the 4.3-a-month rate in the academic study, a club of 7,200 members would see about 1,000 visits a day, versus about 630 at the 10-K-implied rate.

7,200 members paying the lowest published rate ($15 a month plus the $49 annual fee) is about $1.6 million a year; at Black Card prices ($24.99 plus $49) about $2.5 million. The 10-K's $2.0 million average club volume sits inside that range. This is a plausibility check, not a validation.

dossier.angle: Not 'gyms are a scam'. A capacity-and-incentives explanation built only from the company's own disclosed numbers, with the limits of the evidence shown on screen.
